messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Arjun Mehta was a 41-year-old South Asian park ranger who had been in a steady relationship for several years and, until recently, had prided himself on being calm, practical, and hard to rattle. That changed after a period of captivity overseas, an experience he still described only in fragments because the full account felt too shameful and too close. What stayed with him were not stories in sequence but a set of snapshots: a metal door half open, the glare of a fluorescent light, a boot stepping into view, the hard grip on his arm, and the taste of fear in his mouth. When those images came back, they did so as if they were happening in the room with him; at times he could feel the old ache and pressure in the same parts of his body, and at other times he could describe the scene with a flat, numbed distance, as though it had happened to someone else. Even in the early weeks after he returned home, unexpected movement nearby made him flinch as though he were back in danger, and he could not trust reassurance. Friends told him he was safe; his partner said the doors were locked; Arjun still scanned the room, convinced that safety could be taken away without warning. He also began to feel permanently humiliated by what had happened, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and the humiliation deepened his sense that he was set apart from everyone around him.

Those appraisals quickly shaped how he moved through the world. Arjun came to believe that being seen carried risk, so he made himself smaller in public, avoided eye contact, and went along with whatever others wanted because agreeing felt safer than being noticed. He also imposed strict control over what he ate, cutting portions and skipping meals because regulating food gave him one area where he could feel disciplined and not at the mercy of anyone else. At the same time, he found himself replaying scenes of revenge against the people responsible, imagining power reversed and himself no longer trapped. Yet these efforts never settled him for long. The more he tried to control his eating, please others, or mentally punish his captors, the more the images returned in sharper pieces, each flash of the event seeming to confirm how isolated and humiliated he had become. The memory was especially liable to be pulled loose by military topics; if someone at home mentioned the army, or if a news report showed uniforms, his mind jumped straight back to those few terrible moments. Uniforms also set off the same reaction at work, where, as a park ranger, he sometimes encountered law enforcement or search-and-rescue personnel in similar clothing. Being seen in those moments felt exposing, and once he was self-conscious under someone’s gaze, he would think again that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate, which only made the old images more vivid and shameful.

As the months passed, the memory itself started to drive the rest of the cycle. A sudden return of the snapshot images could bring a wave of bodily pain and make him feel as if the captivity were happening again, and once that threat feeling rose he became even more certain that he could not trust safety. When he was jolted by a sound or an abrupt movement on a trail, the room or forest seemed to tilt toward the past, and that sense of danger made the fragments of memory sharper still. The memories, in turn, fed back into his negative beliefs: each return seemed to prove that he remained isolated, permanently humiliated, and somehow at fault. Because he felt that way, he redoubled his efforts to keep control, eating even more strictly, deferring to others, and fantasizing about revenge in private. But these strategies brought their own costs. Skipping meals left him shaky and more reactive to sudden movement, which made the world feel even less safe. Going along with everyone else left him resentful and more aware of being unseen. Revenge fantasies kept his mind circling the captivity long after work, making the images easier to summon and the humiliation harder to shake. And once he was already keyed up, even a uniform at the trailhead, a military comment on television, or a stranger turning too quickly on the path could trigger the same surge of dread and pull him back into the snapshots again.

By the time he sought help, Arjun was still functioning at work but only by keeping himself tightly managed and on edge. His partner had noticed that he was distant at home, jumpy when someone moved unexpectedly, and increasingly unwilling to go out unless he could control the setting. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming trapped in the same private loop every day: the images, the humiliation, the rigid control, the constant scanning. He said he was most afraid that the captivity had permanently changed him, but he was also hoping that therapy might help him feel safe enough to stop living as if danger were always one step away.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to intrusive memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers directly cause his negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette states that appraisals shaped his behavior, but it does not show negative appraisals causing the memory to recur or intensify.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show negative appraisals generating triggers or making him more trigger-sensitive.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows maladaptive strategies increasing memory vividness only indirectly; it does not clearly state that the memory itself leads to those strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows threat feelings rising from the memories, but it does not clearly state threat causing the memory to return or intensify.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat reinforcing safety concerns, but it does not clearly state threat producing negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette describes strategies worsening safety and reactivity, but it does not clearly state the memory causing those maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies create or intensify triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies increase threat or danger feelings directly.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What stayed with him were not stories in sequence but a set of snapshots: a metal door half open, the glare of a fluorescent light, a boot stepping into view, the hard grip on his arm, and the taste of fear in his mouth.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Whenever those details were sparked by a military comment on television or the sight of uniforms at the trailhead, Arjun found himself immediately thinking that the world was not safe and that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate. Those conclusions made the memory more vivid and easier to find, as if the snapshots waited just beneath the surface whenever he judged himself that way.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He also began to feel permanently humiliated by what had happened, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and the humiliation deepened his sense that he was set apart from everyone around him.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That humiliation made him more alert to possible signs that it could happen again; once he had decided he could not trust his own judgment, a raised voice, a stranger turning too quickly, or a uniform in the wrong place could all snag his attention and feel like proof that danger was nearby.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He also imposed strict control over what he ate, cutting portions and skipping meals because regulating food gave him one area where he could feel disciplined and not at the mercy of anyone else.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The memory would come back when he was trying to keep himself controlled, and after it surfaced he would tighten those routines further, telling himself that if he could just stay disciplined enough he might keep the images at bay. But the more he skipped meals and deferred to others, the more he felt that he needed those habits, and the more his life seemed to map itself around the captivity he was trying not to think about.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At the same time, he found himself replaying scenes of revenge against the people responsible, imagining power reversed and himself no longer trapped.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Those scenes were not just fantasies for him; they were what he turned to when the memory broke through, a way of keeping the event in view without feeling helpless inside it. Even so, each time he returned to them, the captivity felt nearer and more dangerous, and he came away thinking that he must still be deeply changed by it.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he tried to control his eating, please others, or mentally punish his captors, the more the images returned in sharper pieces, each flash of the event seeming to confirm how isolated and humiliated he had become.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That constant sense of danger was itself part of the problem: when he felt most on edge, the snapshots came back with extra force, as if his body’s alarm were pulling him closer to the moment rather than away from it. Feeling that threatened also made him more certain that the event had permanently altered him and that safety was something other people got, not him.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even in the early weeks after he returned home, unexpected movement nearby made him flinch as though he were back in danger, and he could not trust reassurance.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because he had come to believe the world was unsafe and that he could not trust his own judgment, almost anything could serve as a trigger: a boot on a trail, a uniform at work, a voice raised on the television, or someone moving too quickly in his peripheral vision. Each of those moments seemed to confirm the same bleak conclusion, and the more certain he became of that conclusion, the more sensitive he was to the next cue.
<<<END>>>
